description_full: Tharisa plc, an investment holding company, engages in the mining, processing, sale, and logistics of platinum group metals (PGMs) and chrome concentrates in South Africa, China, Singapore, Hong Kong, the United Arab Emirates, and internationally. It operates through four segments: PGM, Chrome, Agency and Trading, and Manufacturing. The company sells PGM concentrates, including platinum, palladium, rhodium, gold, ruthenium, iridium, nickel, and copper. It also produces metallurgical chrome concentrate and specialty chrome concentrates; operates a third-party chrome plant, as well as markets and sells the chrome concentrate produced at the plant; and manufactures and sells mining and mineral processing equipment. In addition, the company owns and operates the Tharisa mine, a PGM and chrome mine located on the Bushveld Complex of South Africa. Further, it engages in the research, development, and beneficiation chrome and PGM output, as well as trading of chrome concentrate. Tharisa plc was incorporated in 2008 and is based in Paphos, Cyprus.

financial_summary: THARISA PLC is a small-cap basic materials business with a $415M market cap on $670M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding. Operating margins are contracting by -3.2pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 15% against a 8% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 27%.
The company is burning through $27M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 13× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 4.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 59% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.
